extracted.intended_audience: informed British political readers, members of Parliament, gentlemen and citizens concerned with constitution and public affairs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and normative criteria for judging revolutions, the conduct of political societies, the role of armies and the pulpit, and how to reform or preserve a constitution without destroying constituent institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military organization and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: An armed disciplined body is, in its essence, dangerous to liberty; undisciplined, it is ruinous to society. Armies cannot exist under a divided command.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep armies under a single authority with a simple common oath of fidelity and subject the whole force to regular (annual) inspection. Avoid creating parallel or municipal armies with competing principles of duty, which breed mutiny and render no one responsible for conduct. Examples and anti-patterns: the French practice of balancing crown army with a municipal army produced litigants, pettifoggers, and mutineers; the British model (single authority, common oath, annual inspection) is presented as safer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of civil powers vs unity of military command
rubrics_metrics.description: States may best exist with a partition of civil powers, but armies cannot exist under a divided command.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While civil authorities can be balanced and partitioned, do not apply the same partition principles to military command. Divided military obedience is effectively a state of war or truce rather than peace; it undermines responsibility and discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve constituent parts of the state in political change
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper revolution should remove the man (bad ruler) and preserve the constituent parts of the state (orders, privileges, franchises, law, revenue, magistracy, church).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer reparation and correction of anomalies over wholesale change. Burke contrasts the English Revolution (which 'preserved the constituent parts of the state') with the French case (which he says destroys them while keeping the man). The goal is to secure and strengthen fundamental institutions rather than to level distinctions or dismantle orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine liberty with effective institutions before praising it
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not congratulate a nation on its new liberty until you have seen how that liberty is combined with government, public force, revenue collection, morality, religion, property, peace, order, and civil/social manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liberty in the abstract is not sufficient; examine the circumstances and the use of power by new actors. Burke warns against premature exultation (analogy: not to congratulate a madman or a newly liberated criminal). Prudence requires observing whether new power is used to good ends before offering public praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and accountability of public societies' declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: Public resolutions and addresses should not rest solely on vague authority; signatories and the character of those who speak should be disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A vote or resolution 'stands solely on authority'; the public should know who the signers are so that the value of their opinions can be judged by personal ability, knowledge, experience, and public standing. Anonymous or corporately-phrased addresses risk appearing as political stratagems or frauds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate bounds of pulpit speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Politics and the pulpit are largely incompatible; the pulpit ought to offer the healing voice of Christian charity rather than partisan political harangues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preachers should avoid turning sermons into political manifestos. Burke criticizes Dr. Price's sermon for reviving a pulpit-style that mixes politics and religion (dangerous and novel), and warns that ecclesiastical authority used to promote political doctrines can erode domestic tranquillity. Anti-pattern: using the pulpit to preach doctrines that subtly delegitimize foreign or domestic sovereigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individuals should respect constitutional bounds in foreign correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: A private citizen should not open a formal public correspondence with the actual government of a foreign nation without the express authority of his own government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such conduct is improper and irregular because it risks implying corporate or national authority where none exists. Burke refuses to engage in formal correspondence with a foreign government in any capacity that might be taken as authorized by the British state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate political principles in their circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract political principles (e.g., 'liberty is good') acquire their real effect and value only in particular circumstances, which determine whether they are beneficial or noxious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid metaphysical abstraction when judging political acts; consider how principles are administered, the temper and disposition of actors, and the existing social and institutional context. Burke repeatedly emphasizes that circumstances give colour and discriminating effect to political principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor cautious reform over radical innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Commence with reparation, not with ruin: correct anomalies and settle doubtful questions without impairing the stable, fundamental parts of the constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke praises measures that strengthen the constitution and secure institutions rather than radical changes that destroy established ranks, law, revenue, and magistracy. He views extravagant hatred of innovation as dangerous when it leads to breaking the order of the state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political rhetoric should not covertly propagate abstract doctrines that undermine domestic security
rubrics_metrics.description: Public moralizing or doctrinal claims (e.g., that a sovereign is lawful only if chosen by the people) can serve as slow propaganda to erode existing governmental legitimacy if presented ambiguously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware equivocations and slippery constructions that present dangerous doctrines under plausible or nugatory interpretations. Burke accuses some political preachers of cultivating abstract principles meant to be used later to challenge established governments while avoiding immediate offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess social institutions (church, property, orders) as essential supports for liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Church, property, ranks, corporations, and legal order are integral to the health of the state and to the true enjoyment of liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke argues that England's church and social orders were preserved and even improved by cautious reform; these institutions underpin civil tranquillity and should not be casually upended in the name of abstract freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain military discipline when changing political allegiance
rubrics_metrics.description: Changing whom the army serves (its object of obedience) is permissible only if military discipline and principle are preserved; troops must remain ready for war but not prone to mutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke contrasts the English troops' disciplined shift to support the Prince of Orange (orderly, corps and leaders moving in disciplined bodies) with the French case where troops dragged commanders and committed atrocities. The key is uninterrupted military discipline even when political allegiance shifts.
